 Latino Lubbock ’s Election Day
 “You cannot take this particular audience for granted,” Christy Martinez-Garcia, the magazine’s founder and publisher, said.
 November 10, 2026 
 By Carolina Abbott Galvão 
 AP Photo / Adobe Stock / Illustration by Katie Kosma 
 b 
 Sign up for the daily CJR newsletter . 
 On Election Day, Christy Martinez-Garcia, the founder and publisher of Latino Lubbock , a bilingual monthly, stayed up late to post results on the magazine’s Facebook page. Local returns weren’t expected to come until 4:30am, so it was a long day. But decisions in statewide races were clear much sooner. Democrats James Talarico, the nominee for United States Senate, and Gina Hinojosa, the gubernatorial candidate, won handily, upending decades of Republican dominance in Texas. Talarico is the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988; Hinojosa, Texas’s first Democratic governor to be elected since 1990, will become the state’s first Hispanic governor. “I was like, ‘Wow,’” Martinez-Garcia told me, “‘we are living history.’” 
 Lubbock, a traditionally red city in West Texas home to roughly two hundred and fifty thousand people, nearly 40 percent of whom are Latino, remained a Republican stronghold. A few weeks ago, Talarico and Ken Paxton, his Republican opponent, gathered at venues on opposite sides of Lubbock’s Mackenzie Park to speak before thousands. “On election night Texans are going to prove,” Paxton said , “that America does not belong to those who hate it.” (The last time the county voted for a Democratic president was 1964: Lyndon Johnson, Texas son.) Across the park, Talarico sought to persuade disaffected MAGAites to jump ship, pledging to undo Donald Trump’s tariffs and curtail rising gas prices by ending the war in Iran. “We are welcoming everybody, Democrats, Republicans, and independents alike, into this movement to take back power for working people.”
 Texans, Martinez-Garcia said, were “ready for change.” Many of the crossover votes that helped Talarico and Hinojosa win came from the Hispanic community. Martinez-Garcia, an independent who serves on Lubbock’s city council, told me that she votes for “people, not party.” She thinks Talarico’s appeal lies in his ability to bring people together. “The division, the anger, the attacks, the racism? Enough is enough.” 
 Martinez-Garcia was born in Lubbock. When she was a child, the family moved to the Dallas–Fort Worth area, where they remained until 1970. Then they returned to West Texas, to live next door to her grandfather. Around that time, her parents became community activists; Martinez-Garcia followed suit. 
 Before founding Latino Lubbock , in 2006, Martinez-Garcia was the assistant vice president of communications for UnidosUS, a Washington, DC–based Hispanic civil rights and advocacy think tank, formerly known as the National Council of La Raza. Then she returned home. Her daughter asked why she didn’t see herself represented in media and advertisements around town. “That’s when I just had a little epiphany,” Martinez-Garcia said, “and decided that what I needed to be doing is providing Lubbock news from a Latino perspective.” Today she finances the magazine—which is free to read, claims a monthly readership of a hundred thousand, and has a staff of eight, including part-time contributors—entirely through paid advertisements. In the lead-up to the midterm elections, Republican and Democratic candidates both ran ads in the magazine. (The magazine also once ran advertisements for the Lubbock City Council, but stopped doing so once Martinez-Garcia was elected.) “I appreciated that, because you cannot take this particular audience for granted,” she said of Latinos. “A publication like ours, it’s getting into the neighborhoods, into the locations that these folks go to: churches, coffeehouses.”
 Latino Lubbock reaches people in twenty-three rural communities in the county. “We have folks that come to Lubbock, pick up the publication, and distribute it from there,” Martinez-Garcia told me. Many of those small towns, which also have sizable Hispanic populations, don’t have their own newspaper or print media. In those areas, “we’ve become that resource,” she said. The latest issue features stories on voting rights and the death of Dolores Huerta, the labor leader, as well as a piece on a recent poll showing Latinos swinging away from Trump. Each month, Latino Lubbock publishes three columns: “Forward in Christ,” featuring insights from Josh Ramirez, a local pastor; “COACHing Connection,” on sports news; and “A Teen’s View,” in which a young person writes about what matters most to them. “The heart of everything they do,” Ramirez told me, “is to give a voice to Latino culture as much as possible.” Between issues, Martinez-Garcia posts Facebook updates about community events and reshares major national news. 
 Narratives about Hispanic voters are complex. “People want to lump us together, but we’re so different from each other,” Martinez-Garcia said. Latino Lubbock does not endorse candidates. “My job isn’t to tell people who to vote for,” she said. But the magazine did “remind them to register to vote, make sure they’re aware of the dates to vote, address some of the issues or surveys that are seen on the national level.” Talarico and Hinojosa will both take office in January. In the meantime, Martinez-Garcia has started working on Latino Lubbock ’s December issue: a holiday special. “I’ve seriously been thinking,” she said, “of putting Gina Hinojosa on the cover.”
